What happens when the ground around your bore loses support?
Drill through loose or permeable ground and the fluid pressure in the bore usually runs higher than the pressure in the formation. That's normal, it's what holds the wall open. The problem starts when the fluid can't build a seal against that ground.

In tight, stable formations the fluid naturally plasters a thin cake against the wall and holds pressure. In loose or permeable ground, there's nothing for it to grip. Without that seal, pressure bleeds off into the formation, the wall loses support, and you're looking at sloughing, cave-ins, or fluid loss you can't account for.

So the fluid's job isn't just carrying cuttings out of the hole. It has to swell, plaster onto the wall, and hold that seal for as long as the bore is open.
What ground conditions have given your crews the most grief holding a bore open?

Loose or permeable ground won't hold a seal on its own, your fluid has to do it for you.
HDD Gel is the base fluid we build a stability program around when the ground won't cooperate. It swells and plasters onto the borehole wall, building the seal that holds pressure and keeps the hole open, the same mechanism we walked through Wednesday.

It's not an additive you reach for when something's gone wrong. It's the base you run from the start in unstable or highly permeable ground, so the rest of your fluid program has something solid to work off.

If you're running a bore where wall support is the risk, get the base fluid right first.
Got a tricky ground profile coming up? Call the team, we'll help you build the right fluid program before you spud in.
